LESSONS.title: Final Explanation — Unifying Reflection and Congruence to Solve the Matatu Mirror Mystery
LESSONS.aresKeywords: reflection coordinate rules mirror line equation congruence tests triangle transformation

slo.purpose: Learners synthesise all eight lessons of the sub-strand to construct a complete, written and diagrammatic explanation of why the matatu rear-view mirror produces an image that is the same size and shape as the real lorry yet appears laterally flipped, using coordinate reflection rules and congruence tests as formal proof.
slo.knowledge:
• Reflection maps every object point to a unique image point according to a specific algebraic coordinate rule determined by the mirror line (y-axis: (a,b)→(−a,b); x-axis: (a,b)→(a,−b); y=x: (a,b)→(b,a); y=−x: (a,b)→(−b,−a); y=k: (a,b)→(a,2k−b); x=k: (a,b)→(2k−a,b)).
• The mirror line is always the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining any object point to its image, and its equation can be determined from coordinates of object–image pairs.
• Two triangles are congruent if and only if they satisfy one of the four tests — SSS, SAS, AAS/ASA, or RHS — and a reflected triangle always satisfies SSS with its object, confirming opposite (indirect) congruence.
slo.skills:
• Construct a complete written explanation linking coordinate transformation rules, mirror-line equations, and congruence tests to the matatu mirror phenomenon.
• Compare an initial Lesson 1 model of the phenomenon with a final revised model, annotating every improvement with precise mathematical reasoning.
slo.attitudes:
• Appreciate that mathematics provides exact, universal tools — coordinate rules and congruence tests — that explain everyday phenomena such as driving mirrors, and that this understanding supports road safety.
• Value the iterative process of building, testing, and revising a scientific/mathematical model over multiple lessons.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we use reflection and congruence together to fully explain why the matatu mirror image is flipped yet always an exact copy of the original?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This final lesson closes the inquiry arc: learners move from initial puzzlement about the flipped-but-identical mirror image to a complete, formal explanation grounded in coordinate reflection rules (Lessons 3–6) and congruence tests (Lesson 7), and they revise their Lesson 1 naive model into a mathematically rigorous final model that fully answers the driving question.
slo.safetyNotes: No specific hazards. If small plane mirrors are used during the lesson recap, remind learners to handle glass mirrors carefully and not to direct reflected sunlight into peers' eyes.

LESSONS.overview:
This is the capstone lesson of the Reflection and Congruence sub-strand. Over the previous seven lessons, learners have investigated symmetry, plotted reflections on the Cartesian plane, discovered the four properties of reflection, determined mirror-line equations, constructed reflected images on plain paper, and applied congruence tests to triangles. In this lesson all those threads are woven into a single, coherent Final Explanation that directly answers the driving question: why does a matatu's rear-view mirror show an image that is the same size and shape as the real lorry yet appears flipped — and how can we use this to prove that the original and its mirror image are always congruent?

Learners begin by revisiting their very first (Lesson 1) prediction sketches and written ideas about the mirror phenomenon, then work in groups to construct a formal written and diagrammatic final explanation that incorporates coordinate rules, the perpendicular-bisector property of the mirror line, and a chosen congruence test. The Driving Question Board is completed for the last time: every sticky-note question posted in earlier lessons is reviewed, and learners confirm which have now been answered and celebrate the journey of growing understanding. A whole-class gallery comparison of Lesson 1 models versus final models makes the intellectual growth visible.

The lesson closes with a brief road-safety connection — the matatu conductor's use of mirrors is not just a mathematical curiosity but a life-saving application of reflection and congruence — and with teacher-led consolidation of the six coordinate rules as a reference card learners can keep. The teacher reflection questions guide the teacher to evaluate the quality of learners' final explanations and the coherence of the full storyline across all eight lessons.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner retrieves (or is handed back) their Lesson 1 prediction sketch — the drawing they made of what they thought was happening inside the matatu rear-view mirror. Working individually for 3 minutes, learners annotate their original sketch with two colours: green pen to mark anything they got right in Lesson 1, and red pen to mark anything they now know is incomplete or incorrect. They write one sentence summarising what they were most wrong about at the start of the unit.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the anchoring phenomenon image on the board — the matatu conductor on the Nairobi–Thika highway holding the small rectangular mirror so the driver sees the approaching lorry. Say exactly: 'Before we look at anything new today, I want you to travel back in time to Lesson 1. Take your original prediction sketch. Give yourself 3 minutes of silence to re-read it and annotate it in two colours.' Set a visible timer for 3 minutes. After the timer sounds, cold-call 3 learners (one from each ability band) to share one thing they marked in red: 'Akinyi — what did you get wrong in Lesson 1 that you now know better?' WAIT TIME: 12 seconds after each name before accepting the answer. Write the three 'misconceptions we started with' on the board as a list. Tell the class: 'These are our starting point. By the end of this lesson, each of those should be fully resolved.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Elicit–Confront–Resolve (ECR): surfacing prior conceptions held in Lesson 1 and juxtaposing them with current understanding creates the cognitive contrast that makes final consolidation meaningful. Writing in two colours forces learners to actively distinguish what has changed in their thinking rather than passively reviewing notes.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans annotated sketches as learners work — look for: (1) red annotations that identify at least one specific misconception (e.g., 'I thought the image was smaller' or 'I did not know the image is the same distance behind the mirror'); (2) the ability to name something correct from Lesson 1. Flag learners whose sketches show no red annotation — they may be avoiding self-critique and will need prompting during group work.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of four receive a 'Final Evidence Pack' — a single A3 sheet containing: (a) a Cartesian grid showing a lorry outline (quadrilateral ABCD with given coordinates) reflected in the line x = 0 (the y-axis, representing the mirror surface), with all object and image coordinates labelled; (b) a table of all six coordinate reflection rules studied across Lessons 3–6; (c) measurements confirming AB = A'B', BC = B'C', CD = C'D', DA = D'A'. Learners read and annotate the sheet in silence for 4 minutes, then discuss in their group for 3 minutes: 'Which of the four congruence tests can we use to prove triangle ABC ≅ triangle A'B'C'? Why SSS and not just visual inspection?' Groups record their chosen test and justification in their exercise books.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the A3 Evidence Pack face-down. Say: 'Turn it over — read everything on this sheet silently for 4 minutes. You are detectives. You are looking for the mathematical proof that explains the matatu mirror.' Set timer for 4 minutes. After silent reading, say: 'Now discuss in your group. You have 3 minutes. Answer this one question: which congruence test proves the lorry and its mirror image are identical? Write your group's answer in your book.' Circulate and listen; do NOT answer questions — redirect with: 'What does the evidence pack say about the side lengths?' After group discussion, cold-call 2 groups to share: 'Kamau's group — which test and why?' WAIT TIME: 15 seconds. Confirm SSS is sufficient (all three corresponding sides are equal because reflection preserves length) and note that this is opposite/indirect congruence because the image cannot be superimposed on the object without lifting it off the page — just as the lorry cannot drive through the mirror.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence-Based Argumentation: learners use a structured evidence pack rather than recall, mirroring the practice of a Kenyan engineer reviewing technical data. By requiring a written justification of the congruence test choice, the strategy forces connection between the observed measurements and the formal mathematical claim — a core NGSS Science and Engineering Practice (Constructing Explanations and Designing Solutions).
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher listens for groups that correctly identify SSS and articulate 'opposite congruence' (the image is flipped, so it cannot be overlaid without lifting). Red flag: groups that say 'they look the same' without citing specific equal side measurements — these groups need a targeted question: 'Can you point to the three pairs of equal sides on your grid?'

framework.learnerExperience: Each group constructs a 'Final Explanation Poster' on plain A3 paper. The poster must include four labelled sections: (1) The Phenomenon — a sketch of the matatu mirror setup with the object lorry and its image labelled; (2) The Coordinate Rule — the algebraic rule used (reflection in x = 0: (a,b)→(−a,b)), with one worked numeric example using the lorry's coordinates; (3) The Mirror Line — its equation, and proof that it is the perpendicular bisector of at least one object–image segment (midpoint calculation shown); (4) The Congruence Proof — the chosen test (SSS), three pairs of equal sides named, and one sentence explaining why this is opposite congruence. Learners write a 'headline sentence' at the top of the poster that directly answers the driving question in plain language.
framework.teacherMoves: Give explicit instructions: 'Your poster has exactly four sections — I have written them on the board. Every section must have a diagram AND words. You have 10 minutes.' Write the four section headings on the board with a timer visible. Circulate and use targeted prompts: For Section 2 — 'What is the coordinate rule for reflection in the y-axis? Can you show me with numbers from your grid?' For Section 3 — 'How do you find the midpoint between A(3,4) and A'(−3,4)? What does that midpoint tell you about the mirror line?' For Section 4 — 'Why can't you flip the lorry's image back onto the lorry without lifting it? What is that called?' At the 8-minute mark, say: 'Two minutes left — write your headline sentence first if you have not done so.' After 10 minutes, conduct a 4-minute Gallery Walk: post all posters around the room; each group silently reads two other groups' posters and places a green dot sticker on the most clearly explained section and a question-mark sticker anywhere they are confused. Cold-call one learner per poster to read the headline sentence aloud — WAIT TIME: 10 seconds.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Poster Construction with Gallery Walk: the four-section scaffold prevents superficial responses and ensures every mathematical layer (phenomenon → coordinate rule → mirror line → congruence) is explicitly connected. The Gallery Walk adds peer accountability and exposes learners to multiple representations of the same idea — a powerful consolidation strategy aligned with NGSS Practice 8 (Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information).
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher evaluates poster sections against three criteria: (1) Does the coordinate rule include a numeric example? (2) Is the midpoint calculation for the mirror line shown step-by-step? (3) Does the congruence section name three specific equal side pairs? Collect two posters (from the strongest and the weakest group) for written feedback to be returned in the next sub-strand. Listen during Gallery Walk for misconceptions voiced aloud — e.g., 'I thought the image was bigger' — and address immediately.

framework.learnerExperience: The class returns to the Driving Question Board displayed at the front since Lesson 1. Each learner receives two sticky notes. On the first (blue), they write one question from the board that they can now fully answer, and they write the answer. On the second (yellow), they write one question from the board that they feel is still partially unanswered or leads them to wonder something new. Learners post their notes on the board under two columns: 'Answered ✓' and 'New Wondering 🌟'. The class reads the board together for 2 minutes.
framework.teacherMoves: Point to the DQB and say: 'This board has been with us since the very first lesson. Look at every question we posted. Some were posted by you, some were posted together.' Read three specific questions from the board aloud — choose one from Lesson 1, one from Lesson 4, one from Lesson 7. Then say: 'Take your two sticky notes. Blue note: choose one question you can now fully answer — write the question and write the answer in your own words. Yellow note: write one new wondering — something this unit made you curious about that we did not fully explore.' Give 3 minutes for writing. Cold-call 3 learners to read their blue note answers aloud — WAIT TIME: 12 seconds. After each, ask the class: 'Does the class agree that question is answered? Thumbs up if yes.' For the yellow notes, read 3 aloud and tell the class: 'These new wonderings are the beginning of your next mathematics unit — keep them.' Finally, say: 'Our driving question was: why does the matatu mirror show an image that is flipped yet always congruent? Point to the board — together let us say the answer.' Lead a choral response based on the class's collective headline sentences from the posters.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: DQB Closure with Answered/Wondering Sort: explicitly sorting the board into 'Answered' and 'New Wondering' columns validates the learning journey and models scientific practice — real mathematicians and engineers answer one question and generate three more. The choral final answer builds shared ownership of the explanation and reinforces the vocabulary (reflection, coordinate rule, perpendicular bisector, congruence, opposite congruence) in a low-stakes oral format.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher reads every blue sticky note posted — look for: correct, complete answers that use at least two technical terms (e.g., 'The mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining any object point to its image'). Flag blue notes that are vague ('it goes to the other side') — these learners need individual follow-up. Count the proportion of yellow 'New Wondering' notes that connect to the next sub-strand (Rotation) or to real-life applications — high proportion indicates learners are thinking beyond the immediate task.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open their exercise books to their Lesson 1 model — the initial sketch of what they thought happened in the matatu mirror. They draw a box around it labelled 'Model 1 — Lesson 1'. Immediately below, they draw their 'Final Model — Lesson 8'. The final model must include: a labelled diagram of the matatu mirror setup (object lorry, mirror line, image lorry); the coordinate rule for reflection in the mirror line; the perpendicular bisector property annotated on one object–image segment; and the congruence test (SSS) with the three equal side pairs labelled. In the final two lines of their exercise book entry, learners write: 'My model improved because…' and complete the sentence with at least two specific mathematical ideas gained across the unit.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'The last thing we do today is the most important. You are going to look your Lesson 1 self in the eye and show how far you have come.' Allow 6 minutes for individual model drawing — circulate and use encouraging, specific prompts: 'Wanjiku — I can see your coordinate rule. Can you now add the perpendicular bisector annotation? Remember Lesson 5.' 'Otieno — your diagram is clear. Which three sides did you label for SSS?' At the 5-minute mark, cold-call two learners to share one improvement from their 'My model improved because…' sentence — WAIT TIME: 12 seconds. Write their improvement statements verbatim on the board as a class record. Conclude with: 'The matatu conductor on the Nairobi–Thika highway uses this mathematics every single day — he just does not know he is using SSS and perpendicular bisectors. You now know. That is the power of mathematics.' Assign a closing exit ticket (written on a half-sheet): 'State the coordinate rule for reflection in the line y = x, then write one sentence connecting this rule to the matatu mirror phenomenon.' Collect as learners leave.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model Comparison (Initial vs. Final): placing Model 1 and the Final Model side-by-side in the same exercise book makes intellectual growth concrete and personal. The structured 'My model improved because…' sentence requires metacognitive reflection — learners must identify specific knowledge gained, not just say 'I know more now.' This aligns with NGSS Practice 2 (Developing and Using Models) and the KICD emphasis on learning to learn as a core competency.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect exit tickets as learners leave. Successful exit tickets state the rule (a,b)→(b,a) for y=x AND connect it to the phenomenon (e.g., 'If the matatu mirror were tilted at 45°, the lorry's image would have its coordinates swapped — it would appear above rather than to the left'). Exit tickets that only state the rule without a phenomenon connection indicate the learner can reproduce procedures but has not achieved full conceptual transfer — plan a brief review at the start of the Rotation sub-strand for these learners. Final models in exercise books are reviewed during marking: check for all four required components (diagram, coordinate rule, perpendicular bisector annotation, SSS labelling).

1. Did every group's Final Explanation Poster include all four required sections with both a diagram and a written explanation? Which section was most frequently incomplete, and what does that reveal about where the sub-strand's instructional sequence needs strengthening in future?
2. When learners annotated their Lesson 1 sketches in red during the Predict Phase, what were the most common misconceptions? Were these misconceptions explicitly addressed in Lessons 2–7, or do they suggest a gap in the storyline that should be closed by adding or reordering a lesson?

What differentiated strategy — perhaps a structured 'Because…Therefore…This means that…' sentence frame — would help these learners achieve conceptual transfer rather than procedural fluency alone?

summaryTablePrompt.learned: Reflection maps every point according to a specific algebraic coordinate rule determined by the mirror line; the mirror line is always the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining any object point to its image; a reflected triangle is congruent to its object by SSS and the congruence is opposite (indirect) because the image cannot be overlaid on the object without lifting it — which is why the lorry's headlights appear on opposite sides in the mirror.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The matatu rear-view mirror acts like the y-axis of a coordinate plane: it maps every point on the approaching lorry to a unique image point directly opposite, at equal distance, according to the rule (a, b) → (−a, b). This preserves all lengths and angles, making the image congruent to the lorry by SSS. The lateral flip — the lorry's right headlight appearing on the left — is the signature of opposite (indirect) congruence: the image is a perfect mathematical copy, but it is a mirror copy, not a direct overlay, which is exactly what any flat reflective surface must produce.

FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: You have now completed all eight lessons in the Reflection and Congruence unit. Your task is to write a Final Explanation that answers the driving question: "Why does a matatu's rear-view mirror show an image that is the same size and shape as the real object behind it — yet appears flipped — and how can we use this to prove that the original and its mirror image are always congruent?" Use your Summary Table, your Cartesian plane coordinate work, your flag-construction activity, your congruence-test investigations, and any notes from your Driving Question Board to support your answer. Your response must connect every section back to the matatu mirror phenomenon on the Nairobi–Thika highway. Include specific mathematical evidence: coordinates, distances, angles, and congruence test names (SSS, SAS, AAS, RHS). Use Kenyan contexts and examples where possible (e.g., the lorry's headlights, the matatu conductor's rectangular mirror, shapes found in Kenyan cultural objects). Your complete Final Explanation must be a minimum of 300 words across all sections. Write clearly and precisely — imagine you are explaining this mystery to a classmate who missed the entire unit.

sections.title: SECTION 1: THE MATATU MIRROR PHENOMENON — WHAT DID WE OBSERVE?
sections.prompt: Describe the anchoring phenomenon in your own words. What exactly did the matatu conductor's mirror do to the image of the lorry behind the vehicle? Identify at least THREE specific observations (size, distance, orientation) that made this situation puzzling or interesting. Explain why these observations raised a mathematical question worth investigating.
sections.exemplar:
On the Nairobi–Thika highway, a matatu conductor held up a small rectangular mirror so the driver could see vehicles approaching from behind. When a lorry appeared in the mirror, three things were immediately noticeable. First, the image of the lorry looked exactly the same size as the real lorry — it had not been shrunk or enlarged. Second, the lorry's image appeared to sit as far behind the mirror surface as the real lorry was in front of it — the distances were equal. Third, and most puzzling, the lorry's right headlight appeared on the LEFT side in the mirror, and its left headlight appeared on the RIGHT — the image was laterally flipped, or reversed left-to-right.

This created a genuine mathematical mystery. If the image is flipped, you might expect it to look different — like a distorted or stretched copy. But it did not look different at all in terms of size or shape. Every measurable feature of the lorry — the width of the grille, the height of the cab, the angles of its windscreen — appeared identical in the mirror. So the question became: how can something be 'flipped' and yet remain a perfect copy? This is exactly the puzzle that the mathematics of reflection and congruence helps us solve.

sections.title: SECTION 2: THE FOUR PROPERTIES OF REFLECTION AND THE MIRROR LINE
sections.prompt: Explain the four key properties of reflection that you discovered during the unit. For each property, use precise mathematical language and connect it back to the matatu mirror. Then explain how you can find the equation of the mirror line when you are given an object point and its image point on the Cartesian plane. Include a specific coordinate example in your explanation.
sections.exemplar:
Through our investigations on the Cartesian plane, we established four properties that every reflection obeys. First, the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the line segment joining any object point to its image point — meaning it cuts that segment at exactly 90° and at its exact midpoint. Second, every object point and its image point are equidistant from the mirror line — the lorry is, say, 30 metres in front of the mirror surface, and its image appears exactly 30 metres behind it. Third, points that lie ON the mirror line do not move — they map to themselves. Fourth, the mirror line preserves all lengths and all angles in the figure, which is why the image looks identical in size and shape to the original.

To find the mirror line from coordinates, consider an object point A(2, 6) and its image A'(6, 2). The midpoint M of AA' is ((2+6)/2, (6+2)/2) = (4, 4). The gradient of AA' is (2−6)/(6−2) = −1, so the mirror line, being perpendicular to AA', has gradient +1. Using point-gradient form through M(4, 4): y − 4 = 1(x − 4), which simplifies to y = x. This tells us the mirror line is the line y = x — which we can verify because reflecting any point over y = x swaps its coordinates, exactly as the lorry's left and right sides are swapped in the matatu's mirror. The mirror line is the mathematical 'hinge' of the entire phenomenon.

sections.title: SECTION 3: WHY THE IMAGE IS FLIPPED — LATERAL REVERSAL EXPLAINED
sections.prompt: Explain in mathematical terms why a reflected image appears 'flipped' or laterally reversed. Use the idea of orientation (the order in which vertices appear — clockwise vs. anti-clockwise) to distinguish between direct congruence and opposite (indirect) congruence. Connect this to the paper-template triangle activity: why could you sometimes flip one triangle perfectly onto the other, and why did this sometimes require lifting the triangle off the page?
sections.exemplar:
When you reflect a shape, the image is a mirror copy — every length and every angle is preserved, but the ORDER in which the vertices appear around the shape is reversed. Mathematicians call this a change in orientation. If the vertices of the original lorry outline are labelled A, B, C going CLOCKWISE, then the vertices of the mirror image go ANTI-CLOCKWISE in the same order. This left-to-right flip is called lateral reversal, and it is the reason the lorry's right headlight appears on the left in the matatu's mirror.

In our paper-template triangle activity, we cut two identical triangles from the same template — one representing the 'object' lorry and one representing the 'mirror image.' When we tried to place one on top of the other, we found that for a scalene triangle (one with no lines of symmetry), we could NOT slide or rotate the image triangle to fit the object triangle while keeping both flat on the page. We had to LIFT the image triangle, flip it over, and then it matched perfectly. This is called opposite congruence (or indirect congruence) — the two shapes are congruent, but you need a flip (reflection) to move from one to the other. By contrast, two shapes that can be made to coincide using only slides and rotations (no flip) are called directly congruent. The matatu mirror always produces opposite congruence — the image is a perfect copy that is also a mirror twin.

sections.title: SECTION 4: CONGRUENCE TESTS — PROVING THE MIRROR IMAGE IS ALWAYS AN EXACT COPY
sections.prompt: Explain what congruence means and why it matters in the context of the matatu mirror. Describe ALL FOUR triangle congruence tests (SSS, SAS, AAS, RHS) using clear definitions. Then choose ONE test and use it to formally prove that a triangle in the original lorry outline and its reflected image are congruent. Use specific side and angle labels in your proof.
sections.exemplar:
Two shapes are congruent if they have exactly the same shape and exactly the same size — every corresponding side is equal in length and every corresponding angle is equal in measure. In the context of the matatu mirror, congruence answers the key question: even though the lorry's image is laterally flipped, is it truly an identical copy? The four congruence tests for triangles give us a way to answer YES with mathematical certainty, without needing to measure all six parts of both triangles.

The four tests are: SSS (Side-Side-Side) — if all three sides of one triangle equal all three sides of another, the triangles are congruent; SAS (Side-Angle-Side) — if two sides and the included angle of one triangle equal the corresponding two sides and included angle of another, they are congruent; AAS (Angle-Angle-Side) — if two angles and a non-included side of one triangle equal the corresponding parts of another, they are congruent; and RHS (Right angle-Hypotenuse-Side) — if both triangles are right-angled and share the same hypotenuse and one other side, they are congruent.

Using SSS to prove the mirror image is congruent: Consider a triangle PQR on the lorry's grille outline with P(1,1), Q(4,1), R(4,5). Reflecting over the y-axis gives image triangle P'Q'R' with P'(−1,1), Q'(−4,1), R'(−4,5). By the distance formula: PQ = 3 units = P'Q'; QR = 4 units = Q'R'; PR = 5 units = P'R'. Since all three pairs of corresponding sides are equal, triangle PQR ≅ triangle P'Q'R' by SSS. The matatu mirror always produces a congruent image because reflection preserves ALL distances — this is guaranteed by the four properties of reflection we established in Section 2.

sections.title: SECTION 5: ANSWERING THE DRIVING QUESTION — THE FULL MATATU MIRROR EXPLANATION
sections.prompt: Now bring everything together to fully answer the driving question. Explain in a unified argument: (a) why the mirror image is the same size and shape as the real object, (b) why it appears flipped, and (c) how the congruence tests prove the original and its mirror image are always congruent. Reflect on what was most surprising to you in this unit and describe one place — other than a matatu mirror — where you see reflection and congruence working together in everyday Kenyan life.
sections.exemplar:
The matatu mirror mystery is now fully solved. The image of the lorry in the conductor's mirror is the same size and shape as the real lorry because reflection is an isometry — a transformation that preserves all distances and all angles. Every point on the lorry maps to an image point that is the same distance from the mirror line, on the opposite side, along a perpendicular. Because no stretching or squashing occurs, every length and every angle in the image equals the corresponding length or angle in the original. This is why the lorry's cab looks just as wide and just as tall in the mirror as it does in real life.

The image appears flipped because reflection reverses orientation. The vertices of the lorry's outline, which go clockwise in reality, go anti-clockwise in the mirror. This is lateral reversal — it affects LEFT and RIGHT but not UP and DOWN in a standard rear-view mirror. It is the mathematical reason why, if the lorry had a sign reading 'THIKA,' the mirror would show it as reversed.

Despite the flip, we can PROVE the original and image are always congruent using the SSS, SAS, AAS, or RHS tests. Since reflection preserves all side lengths, SSS alone guarantees congruence for any triangle we choose to isolate from the lorry's outline. The shapes are congruent — they are just oppositely oriented, making this a case of indirect (opposite) congruence.

The most surprising insight from this unit was that 'flipped' does not mean 'different.' A shape and its mirror image are as identical as two mandazi cut from the same dough cutter — they match in every measurement, even if one is face-up and the other face-down. Beyond the matatu, you can see reflection and congruence in the symmetrical patterns on a Kikoi fabric sold at Mombasa market, in the two identical wings of a butterfly photographed at Lake Nakuru, or in the congruent triangular roof trusses of houses being built in Kisumu — every pair of trusses must be congruent to ensure the roof sits level and strong.

rubric.excellent: Excellent (4): Accurately states and explains all four properties of reflection (perpendicular bisector, equal distances, invariant points, preservation of lengths and angles) using precise mathematical language. Connects every property explicitly to the matatu mirror phenomenon with correct coordinate or geometric evidence.

rubric.criterion: Understanding of Lateral Reversal and Orientation
rubric.excellent: Excellent (4): Clearly and accurately explains lateral reversal using the concept of orientation (clockwise vs. anti-clockwise vertex order). Correctly distinguishes between direct congruence and opposite (indirect) congruence. Uses the paper-template triangle activity or a specific shape example to illustrate why a flip is needed to superimpose a reflected image.

Mentions the distinction between direct and opposite congruence, though the explanation may lack full precision or a concrete example.

Does not distinguish between direct and opposite congruence, or confuses the two. Explanation is largely descriptive with no mathematical justification.

rubric.excellent: Excellent (4): Correctly defines all four congruence tests (SSS, SAS, AAS, RHS) with accurate descriptions. Selects an appropriate test and constructs a complete, logically structured formal proof using specific labelled coordinates or measurements that demonstrates the original triangle and its reflected image are congruent. Conclusion is explicitly linked back to the driving question.

Attempts a formal proof using one test with specific labels or measurements; the proof is mostly correct but may have one minor error or omission. Makes a reasonable link between the proof and the matatu mirror context.

Does not attempt a formal proof, or the attempted proof is missing labels, measurements, or a logical structure. The connection between congruence tests and the mirror phenomenon is unclear or absent.

rubric.excellent: Excellent (4): Accurately explains the method for finding the mirror line — using the midpoint of the object-image segment and the perpendicular gradient — and demonstrates the method with a fully worked coordinate example leading to a correct equation. Clearly explains what the equation tells us about the geometry of the situation.
rubric.proficient: Proficient (3): Explains the method for finding the mirror line with mostly correct steps and includes a coordinate example. The final equation may contain a minor arithmetic error, but the method and reasoning are sound. Some explanation of what the equation represents is provided.
rubric.developing: Developing (1–2): Attempts to find the mirror line but the method is incomplete or incorrect (e.g., finds midpoint but does not use perpendicular gradient, or uses an incorrect formula). The coordinate example is missing or contains significant errors. Little or no explanation of the meaning of the equation is given.

rubric.criterion: Coherence, Kenyan Context, and Driving Question Response
rubric.excellent: Excellent (4): The Final Explanation is well-organised, clearly written, and meets the 300-word minimum. Every section connects back to the matatu mirror phenomenon in a meaningful way. At least two specific Kenyan contexts (places, objects, foods, or cultural items) are used as examples. The driving question is answered completely and explicitly in Section 5, integrating evidence from all four content areas.

At least one specific Kenyan context is used. The driving question is addressed in Section 5, though one content area may be insufficiently integrated.
rubric.developing: Developing (1–2): The Final Explanation is below 300 words, poorly organised, or difficult to follow. Connections to the matatu mirror phenomenon are rare or generic. Kenyan contexts are absent or incorrectly applied. The driving question is only partially addressed or not addressed at all in Section 5.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: Why does a matatu's rear-view mirror show an image that is the same size and shape as the real object behind it — yet appears flipped — and how can we use this to prove that the original and its mirror image are always congruent?

lessons.title: Symmetry All Around Us — Anchoring the Matatu Mirror Phenomenon & Lines of Symmetry
lessons.observed: Students observe the anchoring phenomenon: a photograph of a matatu's rear-view mirror showing a flipped but same-sized image of a vehicle behind it. They also examine cut-out plane figures (circles, squares, Kenyan flag outline, leaf shapes) and fold them to locate where the two halves match perfectly.
lessons.learned: A line of symmetry is a line that divides a plane figure into two congruent halves, each of which is a mirror image of the other. Simple figures may have one line of symmetry (e.g., an isosceles triangle), several (e.g., a square has four), or none (e.g., a scalene triangle). The matatu mirror acts as a physical line of symmetry between a real object and its reflected image.
lessons.explained: Teacher note: Use the fold-test as the anchor for the entire sub-strand — if folding along a line produces a perfect overlap, that fold line IS the mirror line. Emphasise that 'same size and shape' is the intuitive entry point to congruence, which will be formalised in Lessons 7–8. Cold-call students to predict how many lines of symmetry the Kenyan flag has before they fold (expected answer: 0 — the shield design is asymmetric; this productive surprise motivates careful investigation). Pedagogical tip: Post the driving question on the classroom wall now and leave it unanswered; tell students every lesson will add one piece of the solution.

lessons.title: Reflection All Around Us — Locating Lines of Symmetry in Plane Figures
lessons.observed: Students systematically fold and draw lines of symmetry on printed outlines of an equilateral triangle, a rectangle, a regular hexagon, and a non-regular quadrilateral. They record their findings in a class table, noting the number of lines of symmetry for each figure.
lessons.learned: An equilateral triangle has exactly 3 lines of symmetry; a rectangle has 2; a regular hexagon has 6; a non-regular quadrilateral typically has 0. A key generalisation: a regular polygon with n sides has exactly n lines of symmetry. Each line of symmetry is also a potential mirror line — the reflected half is an exact, flipped copy of the original half, previewing the properties of reflection explored in Lesson 4.
lessons.explained: Teacher note: Guide students to notice the pattern between the number of sides of a regular polygon and its lines of symmetry before stating the rule — wait at least 10 seconds after posing the pattern question before cold-calling. Reinforce the link to the driving question by asking: 'If we placed a mirror along each symmetry line, what would we see?' Students should articulate that the mirror image would complete the shape perfectly — same size, same shape, but flipped. This is the first verbal rehearsal of congruence language. Avoid introducing coordinate notation yet; keep this lesson purely geometric and visual.

lessons.title: Reflection on the Cartesian Plane — Plotting Object and Image Coordinates
lessons.observed: Students plot a simple triangle with labelled vertices on a Cartesian grid, then reflect it in (a) the y-axis, (b) the x-axis, and (c) the line y = x. They record object coordinates and image coordinates in a two-column table for each case.
lessons.learned: Each mirror line produces a specific, predictable coordinate rule: reflection in the y-axis maps (a, b) → (−a, b); reflection in the x-axis maps (a, b) → (a, −b); reflection in the line y = x maps (a, b) → (b, a). These rules are derived from the data table, not memorised in isolation — students should be able to re-derive them from the pattern they observe. The Cartesian plane gives reflection a precise algebraic language that connects the visual flip seen in the matatu mirror to a mathematical rule.
lessons.explained: Teacher note: Insist that students derive the coordinate rules from their own data tables before the teacher confirms them — this enacts the 'Observe → Explain' learning sequence. A common misconception is that reflection in y = x maps (a, b) → (−b, −a); address this explicitly by having students plot both options and check which one satisfies equidistance from the line y = x. Kenyan context tip: Frame the coordinate axes as 'roads' — the x-axis as Mombasa Road running east–west, the y-axis as Thika Road running north–south — to make quadrant navigation intuitive for Nairobi-based students.

lessons.title: Properties of Reflection — Discovering the Four Rules of the Mirror Line
lessons.observed: Using their plotted reflections from Lesson 3, students measure: (i) side lengths and angles of object vs. image triangles; (ii) perpendicular distances from each object point and its image to the mirror line; (iii) the angle at which the segment joining an object point to its image crosses the mirror line.
lessons.learned: Reflection has four properties: (i) the image is the same size as the object (lengths and angles are preserved); (ii) object and image are equidistant from the mirror line (equal perpendicular distance); (iii) the segment joining any object point to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line; (iv) any point on the mirror line maps to itself (it is invariant). These four properties together define a reflection completely and will serve as the proof toolkit in Lesson 7.
lessons.explained: Teacher note: Property (iv) — invariant points — is frequently overlooked by students; highlight it by asking 'What happens to a point that sits exactly on the mirror line?' (Wait 15 seconds; cold-call two students.) Emphasise that properties (i) through (iii) are what make reflected images congruent — size is preserved because lengths and angles are preserved. Connect explicitly to the driving question: 'We now have the mathematical reason why the matatu mirror image is the same size — can we now prove it is the same shape?' (Leave unanswered until Lesson 7.) Pedagogical tip: Have students write the four properties in their own words before seeing the formal statement.

lessons.title: Finding the Mirror Line — Determining the Equation of the Mirror Line Given an Object and Its Image
lessons.observed: Students are given pairs of congruent triangles on a grid (object and image) without being told the mirror line. They join corresponding vertices, find the midpoints of each joining segment, and draw the line through those midpoints. They then verify the line is perpendicular to each joining segment.
lessons.learned: The mirror line is always the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining any object point to its corresponding image point. To find its equation: (1) calculate the midpoint of the segment joining the object point to its image — this point lies on the mirror line; (2) calculate the gradient of that segment; (3) use the negative reciprocal to find the gradient of the mirror line; (4) substitute the midpoint into y = mx + c to find the full equation. This reverses the process of Lesson 3 and consolidates the perpendicular bisector concept.
lessons.explained: Teacher note: Students often confuse 'midpoint of the segment' with 'midpoint of the mirror line' — clarify that the mirror line extends infinitely; we are only finding one point on it. A useful pedagogical sequence: have students first verify numerically (by measuring distances on the grid) that their constructed line is equidistant from object and image before writing the algebraic equation — this anchors the algebra in the geometric property from Lesson 4. Kenyan context: Frame the task as 'You are a matatu driver; two vehicles are visible in your mirror. Where must the mirror glass be positioned?' — students find the mirror line as the answer.

lessons.title: Constructing Reflected Images — Drawing the Mirror Image of a Flag Outline on Plain Paper
lessons.observed: Students use a ruler and set square (no coordinate grid) to construct the reflection of a simplified Kenyan flag outline across an oblique mirror line drawn on plain paper. They apply the perpendicular bisector property point-by-point: drop a perpendicular from each key vertex to the mirror line, extend it an equal distance on the other side, and join the image points.
lessons.learned: Every object point reflects to a unique image point located by the perpendicular bisector property: drop a perpendicular from the object point to the mirror line, then mark the image at the same perpendicular distance on the opposite side. This construction works for any mirror line orientation — horizontal, vertical, or oblique — and does not require a coordinate grid. The resulting image is congruent to the original object by construction, because every length and angle is preserved.
lessons.explained: Teacher note: This is a practical construction lesson; accuracy matters. Insist students use a sharp pencil and check that their set-square corner is truly 90° before proceeding. A common error is measuring distance along the mirror line rather than perpendicular to it — demonstrate the difference explicitly with an exaggerated incorrect example first. Pedagogical tip: After construction, have students verify congruence by cutting out object and image and superimposing them (allowing a flip) — this tactile check directly answers the driving question at a concrete level and prepares students for the formal proof in Lesson 7.

lessons.title: Congruence Tests for Triangles — Proving the Matatu Mirror Image is Always an Exact Copy
lessons.observed: Students are given four pairs of triangles (each pair congruent by a different test: SSS, SAS, AAS, RHS) and one pair of non-congruent triangles. They measure sides and angles, then decide which congruence test — if any — applies to each pair. They then examine a reflected triangle from Lesson 3 and identify which test applies.
lessons.learned: Two triangles are congruent if they satisfy any one of four tests: SSS (three sides equal), SAS (two sides and the included angle equal), AAS/ASA (two angles and a corresponding side equal), or RHS (right angle, hypotenuse, and one other side equal). A reflected triangle is always congruent to its object because reflection preserves all side lengths (SSS is automatically satisfied). This is the formal proof that the matatu rear-view mirror image is an exact copy of the real object — congruent, not merely similar.
lessons.explained: Teacher note: Distinguish clearly between congruence (same size AND shape) and similarity (same shape, possibly different size) — students frequently conflate these. The key pedagogical move here is to apply SSS to the object–image pair from Lesson 3: all three sides are equal because reflection preserves length (established in Lesson 4, property i). This closes the logical chain started in Lesson 1. Cold-call students to state the full congruence proof in their own words (wait 20 seconds). Kenyan context: Use nyama choma cuts as an analogy — two pieces cut from the same template are congruent regardless of which way they face, just as a reflected triangle is congruent regardless of its orientation.

lessons.title: Final Explanation — Unifying Reflection and Congruence to Solve the Matatu Mirror Mystery
lessons.observed: Students return to the original anchoring photograph of the matatu rear-view mirror from Lesson 1. They annotate it: labelling the mirror line (the glass surface), indicating the perpendicular bisector relationship, writing the coordinate rule that applies, and stating which congruence test proves the image is an exact copy of the real object.
lessons.learned: Reflection maps every point according to a specific algebraic coordinate rule determined by the mirror line; the mirror line is always the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each object point to its image; reflection preserves all lengths and angles (the four properties); and the reflected image is therefore always congruent to the original object (provable by SSS). Together, these four ideas — coordinate rules, perpendicular bisector, preserved properties, and congruence tests — form a complete explanation of why the matatu rear-view mirror shows an image that is the same size and shape as the real object yet appears flipped.
lessons.explained: Teacher note: This lesson is the synthesis lesson; resist the urge to re-teach content. Instead, use structured student presentations — each group annotates one aspect of the photograph (coordinate rule, mirror line equation, properties, congruence proof) and presents to the class. The teacher's role is to connect the presentations into one unified explanation. Pedagogical tip: End by returning to the driving question on the wall poster and cold-calling students to answer it in full sentences — insist they use the four technical terms: reflection, perpendicular bisector, preserved properties, and congruence. This lesson-8 full answer should be qualitatively richer than anything students could have said in Lesson 1, demonstrating measurable conceptual growth across the sub-strand.
